Five Smooth Stones
fyv smooth stohnz
noun phrase (1 Samuel 17)
From the plain English of the Authorized Version, rendering the Hebrew of 1 Samuel 17:40; the stones David chose from the brook to face the giant of Gath.

📖 Biblical Definition

The five smooth stones are the weapons David chose from the brook when he went down to meet Goliath, refusing the armour of Saul and trusting the LORD of hosts. The text records that he took his staff, chose him five smooth stones out of the brook, put them in a shepherd's bag, and with his sling in his hand drew near to the Philistine. The phrase has become a byword for the simple, despised instrument through which God overthrows the proud, for David himself declared that the battle is the LORD'S, who saveth not with sword and spear. The dictionary reads the stones in the line of the apostle: God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty, and the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds. Whether the four unused stones point to Goliath's four giant kinsmen, as some have observed, or simply mark a prudent provision, the great lesson stands: faith does not despise means, for David stooped to gather the stones, yet faith does not trust in means, for the victory is God's alone. The five smooth stones rebuke both the presumption that waits for miracle without effort and the carnal confidence that trusts the sling rather than the LORD who guides it.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The stones David chose from the brook to face Goliath; a byword for the simple, despised means through which God confounds the mighty, neither despising means nor trusting in them.

expand to see more

FIVE SMOOTH STONES, noun phrase. The stones David chose from the brook to slay Goliath (1 Samuel 17:40).

He refused Saul's armour and took sling and stones, declaring the battle to be the LORD'S.

A single stone smote the giant in the forehead and felled him.

Figuratively, the weak and despised instrument by which God overthrows the proud and mighty.

An emblem of faith that uses means without trusting in them, for the victory is of the LORD.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Sa 17:40 — "And he took his staff in his hand, and chose him five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in a shepherd's bag which he had, even in a scrip; and his sling was in his hand: and he drew near to the Philistine."

1 Sa 17:47 — "And all this assembly shall know that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the LORD'S, and he will give you into our hands."

1 Co 1:27 — "But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;"

2 Co 10:4 — "(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Severed from the LORD of the battle, the phrase becomes a motivational emblem of human pluck, as though the stones, not God, won the day.

expand to see more

The popular use of “five smooth stones” has drifted into a slogan of self-reliance and clever underdog strategy, a cousin of the secularized David-and-Goliath trope. The dictionary refuses the drift. David gathered stones, but he conquered by the name of the LORD of hosts; the sling was in his hand, but the battle was the LORD'S. To make the stones the hero is to silence the very confession David shouted across the valley.

The recovery is the biblical balance between means and faith. Faith is not idleness: David stooped to the brook and chose his stones with a shepherd's skill. Yet faith is not carnal confidence either: the apostle teaches that the weapons of our warfare are mighty not in themselves but through God. So the believer labours with the ordinary means God appoints—word, prayer, diligence—while trusting wholly in the LORD who alone gives the victory.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the simple narrative Hebrew of 1 Samuel 17; “smooth” (Hebrew chalaq) marks the stones fit for the sling, gathered from the watercourse of the valley of Elah.

expand to see more

'Eben, Hebrew, a stone, the ordinary word for the missiles of the sling.

Chalaq, Hebrew, smooth, the quality that made the brook-stones fit to fly true.

Nachal, Hebrew, the brook or wadi of the valley of Elah from which they were drawn.

The shepherd's “scrip” or bag marks David's lowly calling, despised by the giant.

The apostolic theme of weak things confounding the mighty (1 Corinthians 1:27) frames their meaning.

Usage

"The pastor warned against preaching the five smooth stones as a lesson in self-confidence, for David trusted the LORD and not the sling."

"He gathered his “five smooth stones” of study and prayer, then cast himself wholly on God for the outcome."

"She learned from the brook of Elah that faith uses means diligently yet trusts only the LORD of the battle."
